content: Waking up for an early morning, brewing up your first coffee for the day, in-between yawns and stretches you might hear a bird chirping just outside your front door. When you hear that chirp, each neuron in your brain has a binary decision to make: do I fire, or do I not fire? Formalized in 1943 by [McCulloch and Pitts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCulloch%E2%80%93Pitts_neuron), inputs arrive, and the neuron fires if the weighted sum exceeds a threshold.

[ReLU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectifier_(neural_networks)) simulates this real brain mechanism in artificial neural networks. Fire if positive, silence if negative. Modern architectures tend to use GeLU or SiLU, but ReLU is a foundational building block and the one we'll look at.

Every token generated by every LLM request runs this activation function once per feed-forward layer, for every layer in the network. [OpenRouter served over 100 trillion tokens](https://openrouter.ai/state-of-ai) in the 13 months ending November 2025. [Google processes 3.2 quadrillion per month](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/sundar-pichai-io-2026/). [DeepSeek-V3](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3) has 61 layers (as a MoE model, only 9 of 257 experts fire per token, but every token still hits all 61 layers). Billions of people, quadrillions of tokens, ~hundreds of layers each, and it's the compiler which decides whether `relu(x + bias)` runs as one kernel or five.

With Python at the top and metal at the bottom, it's the compiler glue sitting in the middle. Its job: lower the human-understandable JAX down to GPU-understandable PTX, a TPU executable, an FPGA bitstream, or a TTNN kernel for Tenstorrent hardware. The code below exports two operations to [StableHLO](https://openxla.org/stablehlo) MLIR: a matrix multiply and an elementwise activation.

python.code:
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax.export import export

def attention_projection(x, w):
    return jnp.matmul(x, w)

x = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((1, 512, 768), jnp.float32)
w = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((768, 768), jnp.float32)

exported = export(jax.jit(attention_projection))(x, w)
print(exported.mlir_module())

annotations.definition: Matrix multiply. Projects each of the 512 token embeddings through the weight matrix. Core op in Q, K, V attention projections.
annotations.why: One call in Python, one op in the output IR. Clean lowering.

annotations.definition: Just-In-Time compile. Traces the function and hands it to XLA. export() only works on jit-compiled functions.
annotations.why: JIT is the bridge between Python and the compiler. Without it JAX runs eagerly and there's nothing to export.

annotations.definition: A tensor's shape and dtype, no actual data. JAX traces the function symbolically using these. No real numbers needed.
annotations.why: Export needs static shapes upfront so the MLIR output can be fully typed at compile time.

annotations.definition: Batch 1, 512 tokens, 768 hidden dimensions. BERT-base hidden size.
annotations.why: 512 is the standard max sequence length for BERT-class models; 768 is the standard hidden dim.

annotations.definition: Square weight matrix. Input and output dimensionality are the same. The projection stays in the same embedding space.
annotations.why: In self-attention, Q/K/V projections preserve the embedding size. In, out, same.

annotations.definition: StableHLO's generalized dot product. Handles matmul, batched matmul, arbitrary tensor contractions.
annotations.why: jnp.matmul compiled to exactly one op. No broadcasting, no reshaping. Clean 1:1 lowering.

annotations.definition: Which dimensions to sum over: dim 2 of the first tensor (hidden) against dim 0 of the second (rows). The inner product of matrix multiplication.
annotations.why: Explicit dimension spec, nothing implicit. The compiler knows exactly what to fuse and parallelize.

annotations.definition: MLIR's static tensor type. Shape [1, 512, 768], element type float32.
annotations.why: MLIR is fully typed at compile time. Shape errors surface before any hardware code is generated.

content: The projection lowered cleanly. One Python call, one [StableHLO op](https://github.com/openxla/stablehlo/blob/main/docs/spec.md#dot_general). The elementwise pass is more interesting.

python.code:
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax.export import export

def elementwise(x, bias):
    return jax.nn.relu(x + bias)

x    = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((1, 512, 768), jnp.float32)
bias = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((768,), jnp.float32)

exported = export(jax.jit(elementwise))(x, bias)
print(exported.mlir_module())

annotations.definition: Rectified Linear Unit. f(x) = max(0, x). Clamps all negative activations to zero.
annotations.why: Introduces non-linearity after the bias add. Without it the whole layer is linear regardless of depth.

annotations.definition: Adds a per-dimension offset to every token embedding. The bias is 768-dim and JAX broadcasts it across all 512 tokens automatically.
annotations.why: Broadcasting is implicit in Python. In the MLIR output you can see what it actually costs: two ops before the add.

annotations.definition: One scalar bias per hidden dimension. No batch or sequence axis. Same bias for every token in every sequence.
annotations.why: Bias is positionally invariant. Each of the 768 hidden units gets its own offset, shared across the sequence.

mlir.code:
module @jit_elementwise {
  func.func public @main(
    %arg0: tensor<1x512x768xf32>,
    %arg1: tensor<768xf32>
  ) -> (tensor<1x512x768xf32>) {
    %0 = stablehlo.broadcast_in_dim %arg1,
           dims = [2] :
           (tensor<768xf32>)
        -> tensor<1x1x768xf32>
    %1 = stablehlo.broadcast_in_dim %0,
           dims = [0, 1, 2] :
           (tensor<1x1x768xf32>)
        -> tensor<1x512x768xf32>
    %2 = stablehlo.add %arg0, %1
         : tensor<1x512x768xf32>
    %3 = call @relu(%2)
         : (tensor<1x512x768xf32>)
        -> tensor<1x512x768xf32>
    return %3 : tensor<1x512x768xf32>
  }

  func.func private @relu(
    %arg0: tensor<1x512x768xf32>
  ) -> tensor<1x512x768xf32> {
    %cst = stablehlo.constant
             dense<0.000000e+00> : tensor<f32>
    %0 = stablehlo.broadcast_in_dim %cst,
           dims = [] :
           (tensor<f32>)
        -> tensor<1x512x768xf32>
    %1 = stablehlo.maximum %arg0, %0
         : tensor<1x512x768xf32>
    return %1 : tensor<1x512x768xf32>
  }
}

annotations.definition: Explicitly expands a tensor along new dimensions by repeating values. Turns the 768-dim bias into a 1x512x768 tensor.
annotations.why: Python's implicit broadcasting made explicit. What looked like one op is actually two broadcasts before the add.

annotations.definition: Elementwise addition across all 393,216 values (1x512x768).
annotations.why: The + in x + bias lands here, but only after both broadcast steps have materialized matching shapes.

annotations.definition: Elementwise max of two tensors. ReLU lowered as max(x, zeros_tensor).
annotations.why: relu is sugar in Python. In MLIR it's explicit: compare every value against 0, keep the larger one.

annotations.definition: JAX preserves function call boundaries when tracing. The Python relu call becomes its own private function in the module.
annotations.why: Function boundaries are a compilation hint. The compiler can choose to inline or keep it separate during optimization.

content: In Python, you can write a single, concise line of code to accomplish something powerful without worrying about the 5 triple kickflips it has to do under the hood to accomplish that something. The kickflips are abstracted away.
One Python expression (`relu(x + bias)`) became two broadcasts, an add, a constant, another broadcast, and a max, when we exported the JAX to StableHLO.

This verbosity is the point - StableHLO makes operations implicit in JAX explicit in IR. Where in Python, broadcasting is invisible, in MLIR it costs two ops. Python's `relu` is sugar, but in MLIR it's `max(x, 0)`, spelled out. It also reveals an optimization opportunity: those five ops: broadcast, broadcast, add, broadcast, and max, each touch every one of the `1 × 512 × 768 = 393,216` values in the tensor independently. A naive backend launches five separate GPU kernels, but a compiler can fuse them into one.
The IR is in hand.
Alrighty. With the MLIR in hand, it's time to convert our MLIR to MLIR.

Our starting point, StableHLO, is a high-level dialect of MLIR, and now we want to take it one step lower - one step closer to the GPU. Where StableHLO describes `what` our JAX wants to accomplish, Linalg dialect describes `how` to accomplish it.
StableHLO ships a build script that compiles MLIR from a known-good LLVM commit. The commit hash lives in `build_tools/llvm_version.txt`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/openxla/stablehlo.git
cd stablehlo
cat build_tools/llvm_version.txt
# 1053047a4be7d1fece3adaf5e7597f838058c947

git clone https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project
cd llvm-project && git checkout 1053047a4be7d1fece3adaf5e7597f838058c947
cd ../stablehlo

sh build_tools/build_mlir.sh ../llvm-project ../llvm-build
```
4,669 compilation units later, MLIR is built. Now configure and build `stablehlo-opt` against it:

```bash
cmake -GNinja -B build \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DMLIR_DIR=../llvm-build/lib/cmake/mlir \
  -DLLVM_ENABLE_ASSERTIONS=ON

cmake --build build --target stablehlo-opt
# [163/163] Linking CXX executable bin/stablehlo-opt
```

With `stablehlo-opt` built, I pointed it at [the MLIR file](https://github.com/src-kearney/remora/blob/38f93c0d0708dbd654059e54d806754b33a4179b/mlir/stablehlo/simple_attention_elementwise.mlir): a bias add followed by ReLU.

```bash
./build/bin/stablehlo-opt simple_attention_elementwise.mlir
```

As shown above, those five elementwise ops (broadcast, broadcast, add, broadcast, max) should be fused into a single kernel. Hoping to collapse the chain, I ran `--canonicalize`, a pass that only applies rewrites which are safe to run anywhere: constant folding, algebraic simplification, nothing that changes program size or surprises downstream passes, only to find the exact same output:

```bash
diff <(./build/bin/stablehlo-opt simple_attention_elementwise.mlir) \
     <(./build/bin/stablehlo-opt simple_attention_elementwise.mlir --canonicalize)
# (no output)
```

So, why doesn't this live in `--canonicalize`? Turns out, there's an actual reason. Google's on-device ML team filed an RFC pushing back on MHLO canonicalizers being too aggressive: folding splat broadcasts is fine for server inference, but it increases model size on mobile and hinders removing unnecessary broadcast ops downstream. The [discussion is public](https://groups.google.com/a/openxla.org/g/openxla-discuss/c/VGBIS0kgPKY?pli=1). MLIR's own canonicalization docs reinforce the principle: repeated applications of patterns should converge, and size-affecting transformations can violate that.
The fold does exist, though. `--stablehlo-aggressive-simplification` has an explicit rule for it:

```
broadcast_in_dim(broadcast_in_dim(X, [dimsA...]), [dimsB...])
  -> broadcast_in_dim(X, merge(dimsA, dimsB))
```
Through folding, we collapse two ops into one - cleaner IR, same semantics. So we want to fold these, right? Seems like a no-brainer.

Folding two broadcasts into one means one fewer op. But the remaining ops still each write a tensor to GPU memory and read it back. _Fusion_, rather than _folding_, eliminates those round-trips. By running all three ops in one kernel, intermediate values never leave the registers. To accomplish fusion, we must lower to Linalg.

```bash
./build/bin/stablehlo-opt --help | grep linalg
```

```
      --convert-elementwise-to-linalg                        -   Convert ElementwiseMappable ops to linalg
      --convert-linalg-to-affine-loops                       -   Lower the operations from the linalg dialect into affine loops
      --convert-linalg-to-loops                              -   Lower the operations from the linalg dialect into loops
      --convert-linalg-to-parallel-loops                     -   Lower the operations from the linalg dialect into parallel loops
      --convert-linalg-to-std                                -   Convert the operations from the linalg dialect into the Standard dialect
      --convert-tensor-to-linalg                             -   Convert some Tensor dialect ops to Linalg dialect
      --linalg-block-pack-matmul                             -   Convert linalg matmul ops to block layout and back
      --linalg-fold-into-elementwise                         -   Fold transpose ops into elementwise
      --linalg-fold-unit-extent-dims                         -   Remove unit-extent dimension in Linalg ops on tensors
      --linalg-fuse-elementwise-ops                          -   Fuse elementwise operations on tensors
      --linalg-generalize-named-ops                          -   Convert named ops into generic ops
      --linalg-inline-scalar-operands                        -   Inline scalar operands into linalg generic ops
      --linalg-morph-ops                                     -   Convert linalg ops between forms
      --linalg-specialize-generic-ops                        -   Convert generic ops back to named ops
      --stablehlo-legalize-to-linalg                         -   Legalize StableHLO to LinAlg
      --tosa-to-linalg                                       -   Lower TOSA to LinAlg on tensors
      --tosa-to-linalg-named                                 -   Lower TOSA to LinAlg named operations
      --tosa-to-linalg-pipeline                              -   The default pipeline for converting TOSA operators to linalg
```

Fortunately, `--stablehlo-legalize-to-linalg` is self-describing: it rewrites `stablehlo.*` ops into `linalg.*` ops the Linalg dialect considers legal. Legalization makes the loops visible - you can't fuse what you can't see.

```bash
./build/bin/stablehlo-opt simple_attention_elementwise.mlir \
  --stablehlo-legalize-to-linalg
```

annotations.definition: Reads the 1D bias at only the last dimension. d0 and d1 are not indexed -- their values are ignored. This is how broadcasting becomes explicit loop indexing.
annotations.why: What Python made invisible, Linalg makes explicit: the bias is accessed at just one index, and the loop nest handles repetition.

annotations.definition: d1 is pinned to 0 regardless of the iterator value. The loop still visits all 512 positions in d1, but this input always reads from row 0.
annotations.why: The second broadcast, spelled out as an indexing rule instead of an op.

annotations.definition: Empty map: no indices. Returns the same scalar value for every iteration of the 3D loop nest.
annotations.why: stablehlo.constant lowers to this: a single captured value read identically at every element position.

annotations.definition: Allocates a new output buffer for this op. Five ops across @main and @relu = five allocations = five passes over 393,216 floats.
annotations.why: This is the cost the fusion pass eliminates.

annotations.definition: All three loop dimensions are parallel -- no loop-carried dependencies, every output element computed independently.
annotations.why: Parallel iterators are also the condition for fusion. The pass can only merge linalg.generic ops whose iterators are all parallel.

annotations.definition: The per-element scalar body. Code here runs once per output element.
annotations.why: After fusion, multiple bb0 blocks merge into one, eliminating the intermediate buffers between them.

annotations.definition: Float add in the arith dialect. stablehlo.add crossed a dialect boundary automatically during --stablehlo-legalize-to-linalg.
stablehlo.constant became arith.constant when crossing into Linalg. Dialect boundaries are crossed automatically by legalization passes.

content: An observant reader would have noticed `--linalg-fuse-elementwise-ops` in my above `stablehlo-opt --help` command. Let's give it a shot, and cross our fingers we see one single, beautiful, fused op.

```bash
./build/bin/stablehlo-opt simple_attention_elementwise.mlir \
  --stablehlo-legalize-to-linalg \
  --linalg-fuse-elementwise-ops
```

annotations.definition: Three operands: 3D input, 1D bias, 3D output. The two broadcast ops were absorbed directly into the indexing maps. No intermediate broadcast buffers needed.
annotations.why: Broadcasting is just an indexing pattern. The fusion pass recognized this and folded the broadcast ops into the combined loop's access maps.

annotations.definition: One allocation in @main, down from three. The two intermediate broadcast buffers are gone.
ReLU against a scalar f32 constant, not a broadcasted zero tensor. The constant was hoisted out of the loop and the zero-tensor broadcast eliminated.
annotations.why: The fusion pass also simplified @relu internally, removing the zero-tensor materialization entirely.

annotations.definition: Function boundaries are opaque to the fusion pass. The add and ReLU live in separate function scopes, so the pass cannot see them as a producer-consumer pair. Running --inline first removes this boundary.
annotations.why: The fix is to inline before fusing.

content: Progress, but not as much dopamine as I was hoping for. The broadcasts collapsed, but the ReLU still lives as a separate op. It turns out, the fusion pass only sees ops within the same function. The add and ReLU lived in separate scopes, so it had no way to know they were a [producer-consumer pair](https://mlir.llvm.org/docs/Dialects/Linalg/#fusion).
Adding `--inline` first copies the ReLU body into @main. Now, the fusion pass can see them together:

```bash
./build/bin/stablehlo-opt simple_attention_elementwise.mlir \
  --stablehlo-legalize-to-linalg \
  --inline \
  --linalg-fuse-elementwise-ops
```

annotations.definition: One allocation. Down from 5 across the unfused version.
3D input, 1D bias (broadcast via index map), 3D output. All 5 StableHLO ops collapsed into a single loop nest.
annotations.why: The 1D bias is accessed by #map1 = (d0,d1,d2) -> (d2), broadcasting across d0 and d1 for free via the indexing map.

annotations.definition: %in is the input element, %in_0 is the bias value at position d2. The broadcast was absorbed into how %in_0 is indexed, not as a separate op.
ReLU inline: clamps the add result to 0 in the same loop body. The relu function is gone -- it was inlined, then fused.
annotations.why: --inline eliminated the function boundary. --linalg-fuse-elementwise-ops then saw the add and relu as a direct producer-consumer pair and merged them.

content: Three off-the-shelf passes: `--stablehlo-legalize-to-linalg` makes ops fusible, `--inline` removes function boundaries, `--linalg-fuse-elementwise-ops` merges adjacent parallel loops.

Before committing to this pipeline, it's worth checking the one of the closest things we have to an answer sheet - [IREE](https://github.com/iree-org/iree/blob/1f3f80891cfe3202b737ae1f12a9d3a803ed1c9f/compiler/src/iree/compiler/DispatchCreation/ElementwiseOpFusion.cpp). Turns out, IREE's `ElementwiseOpFusionPass` calls `linalg::populateElementwiseOpsFusionPatterns` - the same function `--linalg-fuse-elementwise-ops` wraps. The difference is what it passes in:

My pipeline passes nothing. It fuses anything legally fusible. IREE gates every fusion decision against hardware constraints: how many buffers a GPU kernel can accept, whether this crosses a dispatch region boundary, whether this is a broadcast consumer. The mechanism is trivial, the policy is everything.

This exploration was the first step towards something larger: [remora](https://github.com/src-kearney/remora), my attempt to solve the most important problem in the world. That particular problem: figuring out what the most important problem is.
